title: Getting around
goal: Ask for and give directions, take a taxi, rickshaw or bus, and tell people what to do with polite and informal commands.
intro:
Street names are little used in Pashtun towns: directions are given by landmarks — the mosque, the bazaar, the bridge, the crossroads — and people are happy to walk you halfway there. In Peshawar you'll ride in auto-rickshaws (رکشه) and colourful buses; in Afghan cities in yellow-and-white taxis and minibuses that leave from an **اډه** (stand) when full.

In this unit you'll learn transport and town vocabulary, the **imperative** (go! come! stop!), and the little words for 'to', 'from' and 'up to'.

grammar.title: The imperative: commands and requests
grammar.body:
The imperative is the verb stem + **-a** (to one person, informal) or **-əy** (polite or plural). As with other verb forms, it can be imperfective or perfective.

**Perfective** (the usual choice for a single action): وګوره wə́gora 'look!', وخوره 'eat!', وکړه 'do!', راشه rā́sha 'come!', لاړ شه lāṛ sha 'go!', کېنه kéna 'sit!'. Polite: وګورئ، وخورئ، وکړئ، راشئ، لاړ شئ، کېنئ.

**Imperfective** (for general or ongoing instructions): ورو ځه 'go slowly (keep going slowly)', ليکه 'keep writing'.

**Negative**: **مه** (ma) + the **imperfective**: مه ځه 'don't go', مه کوه 'don't do it', مه ودرېږئ 'don't stop'.

Politeness comes from -əy, from مهرباني وکړئ 'please', and from tone — a bare command to an elder is rude, so add a title: حاجي صاحب، کېنئ.

grammar.title: To, from, up to: direction words
grammar.body:
Direction is shown with adpositions around or after the noun (which is in the oblique):

**… ته** ta — to, towards: ښار ته 'to the city', ما ته 'to me'
**له … نه** (or **له … څخه**) — from: له کابل نه 'from Kabul'
**تر … پورې** — as far as, until: تر پله پورې 'as far as the bridge', تر سبا پورې 'until tomorrow'
**په … کې** — in, at (unit 6)

Note: after له and تر, masculine nouns ending in a consonant often take the old **ablative ending -a**: له کوره 'from home', تر بازاره 'up to the bazaar', له ښاره 'from the city'. Both له کور نه and له کوره are fine.

'Home' as a destination is simply کور ته, and 'where to?' is چېرته؟ or کوم لور ته؟

dialogue.title: A rickshaw in Peshawar
dialogue.setting: Tom, a visitor, needs to get from his guesthouse to the Qissa Khwani bazaar. He stops a rickshaw.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: السلام عليکم، وروره! قصه خوانۍ ته ځې؟
lines.roman: assalā́mu ʿaláykum, wróra! qisa xwānə́y ta dze?
lines.en: Hello, brother! Will you go to Qissa Khwani?

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.en: Yes, I'll go. Come, get in.

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.native: نه ډېر. شل دقيقې لار ده، خو په سړک ډېر موټر دي.
lines.roman: na ḍer. shəl daqiqé lār da, xo pə saṛák ḍer moṭár di.
lines.en: Not very. It's twenty minutes, but there are lots of cars on the road.

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.native: مه وېرېږه، ښه چلوونکی يم! ته د کوم ځای يې؟
lines.roman: ma weréẓa, ṣə chalawúnkay yəm! tə də kum dzāy ye?
lines.en: Don't worry, I'm a good driver! Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: له امريکا نه يم. ما تر بازاره پورې بوځه، بيا پياده ګرځم.
lines.roman: la amrikā́ na yəm. mā tər bāzā́ra póre bódza, biyā́ piyā́da gə́rdzəm.
lines.en: I'm from America. Take me as far as the bazaar, then I'll walk around.

lines.speaker: Driver
lines.native: دا قصه خوانۍ ده. دلته ودرېږم؟
lines.roman: dā qisa xwānə́y da. dálta wədréẓəm?
lines.en: This is Qissa Khwani. Shall I stop here?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.native: هو، د هغه جومات مخې ته ودرېږه. ډېره مننه!
lines.roman: ho, də haġə́ jumā́t mə́xe ta wədréẓa. ḍéra manə́na!
lines.en: Yes, stop in front of that mosque. Thanks a lot!

culture: Peshawar's **Qissa Khwani** ('storytellers') bazaar takes its name from the travellers and traders who once gathered there to swap tales over tea. In both Afghanistan and Pakistan it's normal to agree the fare before a rickshaw or taxi ride — ask څو روپۍ؟ / څو افغانۍ؟ first. Men and women are usually seated separately on buses (women at the front). Ask directions from shopkeepers or older men; if you need help as a woman, it's natural to approach a woman or a family. Many people give directions by pointing and saying 'over there' (هلته، هغه خوا), so it helps to repeat the landmark back: جومات ته نږدې؟
